subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Fundamental Concepts and Sources of Shari'ah
Islamic Finance in Pakistan and the Islamic Economy
Islamic Economic System and Distribution of Wealth

subjective.topic: Fundamental Concepts and Sources of Shari'ah
subjective.question: Define Deen, Shari'ah and Fiqh, and distinguish between them.
subjective.answer: Deen is the recognition of the universal system and living a life in harmony with it. Shari'ah is the general framework that Islam as a religion prescribes to its believers to lead a life in complete submission to Allah. Fiqh is the understanding of the Shari'ah requirements used to draw the specific rules and regulations required to lead a life in complete submission to Allah. As regards their scope, Deen is very generic in its form, Shari'ah is a specific form of it, and Fiqh is the framework and rule book drawn from Shari'ah.

subjective.topic: Fundamental Concepts and Sources of Shari'ah
subjective.question: What are the four fundamental sources of Shari'ah? Explain each briefly.
subjective.answer: The four fundamental sources of Shari'ah are: (1) The Holy Quran — the revealed book, preserved today in its original form; it is not a rule book but offers general guidance except in a few cases. (2) Sunnah — the recorded sayings and actions of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him); the books of Ahadeeth provide detailed guidance on what a Muslim can do and cannot do, and how to do certain things. (3) Ijma' — consensus amongst scholars of a given generation on certain matters on which there is no unambiguous guidance either in the Holy Quran or in Sunnah; in the contemporary context, the rulings issued by the Fiqh Academy of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) are deemed as Ijma'. (4) Qiyas — a technique to accept or reject new things and phenomena based on their similarities with an already prohibited or accepted thing or phenomenon; it is applicable only when there is no precedence in the previous three sources.

subjective.topic: Fundamental Concepts and Sources of Shari'ah
subjective.question: What is Ijtihad? Who can exercise it?
subjective.answer: Ijtihad is the process of deriving new rulings on something new on which all the sources of Shari'ah are quiet (silent). It can be exercised by only qualified experts, who are called Mujtahid.

subjective.topic: Fundamental Concepts and Sources of Shari'ah
subjective.question: Name the major schools of Islamic legal thought and state where each school predominantly prevails.
subjective.answer: The major schools of Islamic legal thought are Hanafi, Shafa'ii, Hanbali, Maliki and Ja'afari/Zaidi, besides others. The Hanafi school is the largest and predominates in the Indian sub-continent, Turkey and the Central Asian countries. The Shafa'ii school is the second largest and predominates in Egypt, Malaysia etc. The Hanbali school predominates in Saudi Arabia, while the Maliki school predominates in Sudan and the North African countries.

subjective.topic: Islamic Finance in Pakistan and the Islamic Economy
subjective.question: Describe the development of Islamic banking and finance in Pakistan.
subjective.answer: The demand for an Islamic economic system in Pakistan grew out of the literature of the Ulama and the first generation of Islamic economists, supported by political demand and constitutional recognition. In the early 1960s, an Islamic cooperative bank was set up in Karachi that failed within 6 months. In the 1980s, the then military government announced the conversion of the entire banking system to Islamic, and the Modaraba Companies and Modaraba (Floatation and Control) Ordinance 1980 was promulgated; the 1990s was the decade of struggle for the Islamisation of the banking system. From 2000 onwards, the first full-fledged Islamic bank was established in 2002; now 5 fully-fledged Islamic banks are operating in the country, 17 conventional banks are operating Islamic windows, and there is a vibrant Islamic fund management industry, issuance of Sukuk, Takaful companies and Islamic microfinance services.

subjective.topic: Islamic Finance in Pakistan and the Islamic Economy
subjective.question: What is an Islamic economy? State the role of Islamic banking and finance in an Islamic economy.
subjective.answer: An Islamic economy is an economy that operates on the principles of Islam governing economic activities, while Islamic economics is the study of the behaviour of all the economic actors in an Islamic economy. Its institutions include the state, the social sector, the private sector and international institutions. The role of Islamic banking and finance in such an economy is the mobilisation of savings and the financing of economic activities. It is not the role of Islamic banks to contribute to social goals like poverty eradication; for this, other Islamic financial institutions like Awqaf and specialised development finance institutions are required.

subjective.topic: Islamic Finance in Pakistan and the Islamic Economy
subjective.question: How does an Islamic bank differ from a conventional bank?
subjective.answer: A bank is a financial intermediary which collects deposits and offers credit. A conventional bank deals in credit on the basis of interest, whereas an Islamic bank offers financing rather than credit, through Shari'ah-compliant contracts such as sale, lease and partnership. An Islamic bank should indeed be different from a conventional one — after all, it is Islamic; however, despite all the differences, an Islamic bank will always look like a bank: it may behave differently, but its fundamental value proposition will be that of a bank.

subjective.question: Define Riba. What exactly is prohibited in Riba?
subjective.answer: In its simplest form, Riba is the difference of quantities in unequal exchange of anything; it applies to anything and everything, not just money. While inequality of exchange is the essence of Riba, what is prohibited in it is compulsion: if one party compels (or makes the other agree) to pay an additional amount in an exchange, that is considered as Riba. A unilateral payment (without prior agreement) of an additional amount is not Riba; rather, it may be considered as a gift.

subjective.question: Define Gharar and explain what is prohibited in the name of Gharar.
subjective.answer: In its simplest form, Gharar is the lack of knowledge of, and explicit agreement on, the terms and conditions in a contract. Some people argue that the prohibition of Gharar also covers general uncertainty and speculation. What is actually prohibited is contractual uncertainty, and not uncertainty itself: any uncertainty or ambiguity that may lead to dispute and disagreement is prohibited.

subjective.question: Define Maysir. Why is it prohibited?
subjective.answer: In its simplest form, Maysir is gambling. Gambling takes place if two or more people pool their money to reward one of them, or all of them, unproportionate to their individual contributions, based on the result of a game or a random process or event. It is prohibited because it rewards a person unproportionate to his contribution on the basis of a random event, and because the loss of one person is the gain of the other — it is a zero-sum game.

subjective.question: Explain the economic rationale for the prohibition of Riba and its ill effects.
subjective.answer: Riba involves inequality: one party gives more than the other in an exchange, and the question arises where the additional amount would come from. In the case of the exchange of money in unequal quantities, i.e. on the basis of interest, the money will eventually lose value. If everyone continues to charge interest from everyone else, a debt bubble comes into being, diluting everyone's ownership of money, and inflation is another consequence of the interest-based lending system. Anything that is value-reducing cannot be welfare enhancing; in fact, interest amounts to expropriating other's wealth unjustly, which is the real rationale for the prohibition of interest.

subjective.question: "Bank interest is not prohibited; only interest on consumption loans is Riba." Discuss this controversy.
subjective.answer: This claim is wrong. The basic form of Riba involves charging a penalty for default, and all interest loans by banks contain a default penalty; therefore bank interest is Riba. Similarly, the related misconceptions are also wrong: interest cannot be charged to cover the loss due to inflation, because inflation is a macro phenomenon and the borrower should not be penalized for it; and Riba does not cover only usury or only compound interest — most of the English translations of the term Riba in the past wrongly translated it to usury. There has never been any genuine misunderstanding around Riba or its meanings and scope.

subjective.question: What is a contract in Islamic law? State the conditions of a valid contract.
subjective.answer: A contract is a mutual agreement between two or more parties to do something Shari'ah compliant as per agreed terms and conditions. The contract is the basis of all dealings in Islam; nothing can go beyond the scope of a contract, whether it is buying and selling, renting or giving something for free, and Muslims are bound by their contracts, whether implicit or explicit. A valid contract must be between two independent individuals (sane, adults and free) who should agree on the price and its payment and the delivery of the object of sale, which must be halal. Any ambiguity in the transactors, price and object of sale may invalidate the transaction due to the existence of Gharar.

subjective.question: What is a spot (base level) contract? Why is it considered Gharar-free?
subjective.answer: A base level contract in Islamic law is a spot contract. A spot sale contract involves spot payment of price by the buyer to the seller, who must deliver the object of sale immediately. Such a contract is Gharar-free as everything is known: known transactors, known price and known object of sale. In the other variants of a contract, only one of the two countervalues may be delayed but not both: if the price is delayed, the delivery of the sold item cannot be deferred, and vice versa; however, the delayed price should be known, and the deferred sold item must be known with all its attributes and quantity.

subjective.question: Classify Islamic contracts into their categories, giving examples of each.
subjective.answer: There are five categories of Islamic contracts, besides some other contractual arrangements: (1) Sale contracts — spot sale, deferred payment contract (Bai' Mu'ajjal), deferred delivery contract (Bai' Salam), commissioned sale/purchase contract (Bai' Istisna') and cost-plus contract (Murabaha). (2) Lease contracts — simple lease (Ijara), hire purchase (Ijara Muntahiya Bittamlik), forward lease (Ijara Mausufa Fidzimma) and lease with gift (Ijara wa Iqtina'). (3) Investment contracts — Musharaka and Mudaraba. (4) Supporting contracts — agency (Wakala), Juala (service agency), guarantee (Kafala), pledge (Rehn) and remittance (Hawala). (5) Gratuitous contracts. Other contractual arrangements include Wa'ad, Tawarruq, Takaful, Sukuk and Tahawwut.

subjective.question: State the rules about the sale and purchase of money in Islam.
subjective.answer: There are stricter rules for dealing in money. Currencies can be bought and sold, but only on spot: in an exchange of money for money, both countervalues must be equal and must be exchanged on the spot, because any excess on either side is Riba. This is why, for example, Musharakah certificates representing only cash can be sold only at par value.

subjective.question: What are the basic rules of trade (sale) in Islam?
subjective.answer: In Islam, trade is the basis of business, and all Fiqhi literature on business is about buying and selling; this is perhaps the reason that Islamic banking and finance also relies on trading or the financing of trading activities. There is no upper limit on earning profit as long as there is no monopoly power and no market manipulation takes place. Anything and everything can be bought and sold, except haram goods and services, goods and services that are non-existent, and goods and services not owned by the seller. Public goods such as air, water and the right of passage cannot be bought and sold.

subjective.question: Differentiate between Bai' Mu'ajjal, Bai' Salam and Bai' Istisna'.
subjective.answer: In Bai' Mu'ajjal (deferred payment sale), the delivery of the goods is immediate but the price is deferred to a future date; the price could be paid in easy instalments and the deferred price could be higher than the spot price. In Bai' Salam (deferred delivery sale), the price is paid in advance and the delivery of the goods is deferred to a future date; it was historically used for the sale of agricultural produce. Bai' Istisna' is a commissioned manufacturing contract, in which an item is ordered to be manufactured or constructed (e.g. a house, a ship or furniture on order); the price is paid in instalments while the object of sale is delivered once it is ready.

subjective.question: What is Salam? State its main features and conditions.
subjective.answer: Salam is a deferred delivery sale in which the price is paid in advance and the goods are delivered later. It was historically used for the sale of agriculture produce: for the seller it is a tool for generating liquidity upfront, and for the buyer it is part of risk management for ensuring adequate supply in future. The Salam price is normally lower than the prevailing market price. Salam can be applied to generic items only — a specific item cannot be bought and sold on a Salam basis. Like in any other Islamic sale contract, the Salam price cannot be changed once it has been agreed; for example, if the seller is unable to deliver the product in time, the Salam price cannot be reduced by the buyer. Salam is now used by Islamic banks all over the world, and countries like Sudan are known for their Islamic banks using Salam for financing farming.

subjective.question: What is Istisna'? How is its price paid, and where is it used in Islamic finance?
subjective.answer: Istisna' is a commissioned manufacturing sale, relevant to activities like the construction of homes and commercial buildings, ship building and the like; it can even be used for buying furniture 'on order'. The price is paid in instalments while the object of sale is delivered once it is ready. For example, a construction company offers to sell the houses it plans to build; buyers pay some money in advance and a certain amount every quarter subject to satisfactory construction, and after the house is ready, possession is given to the buyers, by which time they have paid the whole price. Istisna' is being used in Islamic finance in a number of structures like Sukuk, project finance and a number of other infrastructure projects.

subjective.question: Explain Bai' 'Ina and discuss its Shari'ah status.
subjective.answer: Bai' 'Ina is a buy-back sale. It is actually a combination of two sales: in the first sale, a seller sells something to a buyer on a deferred payment basis for price P1; immediately, the buyer (now seller) sells the same thing back to the first seller for price P2 on a cash basis, where P2 is less than P1. The end result is that it becomes a financing facility, in which the first party receives financing of P2 for a financing cost of P1 minus P2. Bai' 'Ina is not accepted as a permissible sale by most of the Schools of Islamic Law, except a minority view held by Shafa'ii in Malaysia; it was heavily used in Islamic banking and finance in Malaysia but is now being phased out. It is a valid contract if implemented properly, but it remains a controversial contract.

subjective.question: What is meant by the time value of money in Islam? Can deferment be priced?
subjective.answer: Time Value of Money is not recognized in Islam; time is, however, valued. The deferment of the price of a sold item may be priced — for example, in Bai' Mu'ajjal the deferred price could be higher than the spot price. However, the pricing of deferment of debt is strictly prohibited, because once a debt is established, any increase charged for giving more time is Riba.

subjective.topic: Islamic Economic System and Distribution of Wealth
subjective.question: What are the three objects of the Islamic theory of the distribution of wealth?
subjective.answer: The three objects of the Islamic theory of the distribution of wealth are: (1) the establishment of a natural system of economy; (2) securing for everyone what rightfully belongs to him; and (3) eradicating the concentration of wealth, i.e. wealth, instead of becoming concentrated in a few hands, should be allowed to circulate in the society as widely as possible, so that the distinction between the rich and the poor is narrowed down as far as is natural and practicable. Islam has not permitted any individual or group to have a monopoly over the primary sources of wealth, such as mines, forests, un-owned barren lands, hunting and fishing, wild grass, rivers and seas; every member of the society has an equal right to derive benefit from them.

subjective.topic: Islamic Economic System and Distribution of Wealth
subjective.question: Compare the Islamic view of the factors of production with the capitalist view.
subjective.answer: Under Capitalism there are four factors of production — land, labour, capital and entrepreneur — and land receives rent, labour receives wages, capital receives interest and the entrepreneur receives profit. From the Islamic point of view: (1) the entrepreneur, as a regular factor, has been excluded from the list, and only three factors are recognized; the entrepreneur is not an independent factor but is included in any one of the three factors. (2) It is not 'interest' but 'profit' that has been considered as the reward for Capital. (3) 'Capital' includes only those things which cannot be utilized without being wholly consumed and which cannot be let or leased, for example money; machinery is excluded from Capital. (4) 'Land' is defined in a more general way, covering all those things which do not have to be wholly consumed in order to be used, so machinery too falls under this category. (5) The definition of Labour is generalized so as to include mental labour and planning. Islam also recognizes two kinds of right-holders in wealth: those who have directly participated in the production of wealth, and those to whom Allah has made it obligatory upon others to help.

subjective.topic: Islamic Economic System and Distribution of Wealth
subjective.question: Why does Islam encourage the circulation of wealth? How does its position differ from Capitalism and Socialism?
subjective.answer: Circulation of wealth is encouraged in Islam so that wealth does not become concentrated in a few hands and the distinction between the rich and the poor is narrowed. Capitalism affirms an absolute and unconditional right to private property, which leads to the concentration of wealth. Socialism totally denies the right to private property and distributes wealth only in the form of wages; but surrendering all capital and land to the state merely replaces many smaller capitalists with a single big capitalist — the state — and injures both the establishment of a natural system of economy and securing for everyone what rightfully belongs to him. Islam lies between the two extremes: it admits the right to private property but not as an absolute and unconditional right; it distributes wealth in the form of profit and rent as well as wages, has put an interdiction on interest, and has prescribed a long list of the people who have a secondary right to wealth, thus eradicating the concentration of wealth.

subjective.question: Define Mudarabah. Who bears the loss in a Mudarabah contract?
subjective.answer: Mudarabah is a contract of co-operation between capital and work (organization): one person invests capital while another manages the business, and each has a share in the profit. The person who invests his capital is called Rab-ul-Maal and the person who manages the business is called Mudarib. The profit is shared between them according to a pre-agreed ratio, while the financial loss, if any, is borne by the Rab-ul-Maal alone; the Mudarib loses his labour and effort. Mudarabah is used by banks, for example, for import financing where a letter of credit is opened without any margin.

subjective.question: Define Musharakah. How are profit and loss shared in it, and why is it called the ideal mode of financing?
subjective.answer: Musharakah is a partnership (Shirkat-ul-Aqd) in which the partners jointly invest capital in a business and jointly share its profit and loss. The profit may be distributed in an agreed ratio, which may differ from the ratio of investment, but the loss must be borne by the partners in exact proportion of their respective investments. Musharakah is regarded as the ideal mode of financing because it is based on equity participation and the sharing of risk between the financier and the business, instead of a fixed return on a loan; it can be used for project financing, financing of a single transaction, financing of working capital and can also be securitized through Musharakah certificates.

subjective.question: When can Musharakah certificates be traded in the secondary market?
subjective.answer: Musharakah certificates represent the holder's proportionate ownership in the assets of the Musharakah. Trading in these certificates is not allowed when all the assets of the Musharakah are still in liquid form (cash, receivables or advances due from others); in that case a certificate can be sold only at par value, because money exchanged for money must be equal and any excess is Riba. Once the project has acquired substantial non-liquid assets, the certificates may be bought and sold at any agreed price, since the subject matter of the sale is a share in tangible assets. For example, a certificate of face value Rs. 100 representing 60% liquid and 40% non-liquid assets may be sold at any price more than Rs. 60, but never at Rs. 60 or less. Most contemporary scholars allow trading only if the non-liquid assets are more than 50% of the total worth, so for trading acceptable to all schools the portfolio must consist of non-liquid assets valuing more than 50% of its total worth; under the Hanafi view, trading is allowed even below 50%, provided the non-liquid assets are not negligible.

subjective.question: How can Musharakah and Mudarabah be used for financing a single transaction, such as an import?
subjective.answer: Musharakah and Mudarabah can be used easily for financing a single transaction, and can be employed for financing imports and exports. An importer can approach a financier to finance a single transaction of import alone on the basis of Musharakah or Mudarabah. If the letter of credit is opened without any margin, the form of Mudarabah can be adopted; if the L/C is opened with some margin, the form of Musharakah, or a combination of both, will be relevant. After the imported goods are cleared, their sale proceeds are shared by the importer and the financier according to a pre-agreed ratio, and the ownership of the imported goods remains with the financier to the extent of the ratio of his investment. This Musharakah can be restricted to an agreed term; if the goods are not sold by the expiry of the term, the importer may himself purchase the share of the financier at the market rate, or at a price agreed between the parties on the date of sale, and not at a pre-agreed price.

subjective.question: Explain the running Musharakah account on the basis of daily products.
subjective.answer: A running Musharakah account may be operated on the basis of daily products according to the following procedure: (i) a certain percentage of the actual profit must be allocated for the management; (ii) the remaining percentage of the profit must be allocated for the investors; (iii) the loss, if any, should be borne by the investors only in exact proportion of their respective investments; (iv) the average balance of the contributions made to the Musharakah account, calculated on the basis of daily products, shall be treated as the share capital of the financier; and (v) the profit accruing at the end of the term shall be calculated on the daily product basis and distributed accordingly. In effect, the profit accrued to the Musharakah portfolio is divided on the capital utilized per day: the average profit earned by each rupee per day is multiplied by the number of days each investor has put his money into the business, which determines his profit entitlement.
